attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The revised proposition keeps the claimed mechanism, his reason ('a computer could theoretically do it') and his concession ('even if the work product sucks'). Treating it as a causal claim about executive behaviour fits.

contract.note: Counting informal managerial devaluation, not only formal reclassification, and reading 'more and more' as a growing pattern is an ordinary reading. The 2023 period up to publication is the evaluator's choice but a reasonable one.

evidence.note: OECD case studies from interviews completed in 2022. They describe some lower skill needs after automation but warn that this is not overall deskilling. The period is too early and the study does not test the generative-AI mechanism or the poor-output condition.

reviews.rationale: The only item is pre-2023 workplace research. It neither shows nor rules out executives treating skilled work as unskilled during 2023 because of perceived AI substitutability despite poor output. The packet has no matched corporate records or longitudinal evidence, so the claim cannot be settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'Will be used' is an unhedged forecast with no deadline. The proposition keeps both alternatives joined by 'or' and the 'regardless of how capable' qualifier.

contract.note: Reading 'entire roles' as whole positions at an employer and requiring rollout despite real shortcomings is a fair, ordinary reading. Letting one documented case after publication resolve the claim is lenient but defensible for an open-ended forecast with no stated prevalence.

evidence.note: The Verge (Sep 2023) reports that G/O Media laid off the Gizmodo en Español editors on Aug 29, 2023, after publication, and switched to automatic AI translation. Readers saw translated articles switch into English partway through. This shows whole-team replacement despite poor output.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met through the replacement route. On Aug 29, 2023, after the post, G/O Media eliminated its Spanish-language editorial team and replaced it with AI translation that visibly malfunctioned. That establishes both role replacement and deployment despite capability shortcomings. The workload route does not need to be shown.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words; the 'reasonable person' is a rhetorical setup he then rejects.

semantics.note: Adding 'via AI' matches the surrounding paragraph. The claim is an observation that companies accept lower quality for expected savings.

contract.note: Requiring evidence that links accepting poor output to an expected cost saving is a fair reading of 'to theoretically save a dollar'. The July 2023 window is the evaluator's choice but reasonable.

evidence.note: Vox reports error-filled G/O AI articles and continued executive interest, and notes that AI content costs very little. The cost motive is the reporter's analysis, not a management admission.
G/O executives say they aim to hire more journalists and promise editor review in future. This cuts against an explicit choice of quality for savings, but these are management's own statements.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows defective AI output and a plausible cost incentive. Nothing in it ties management's acceptance of lower quality to expected savings, which the contract requires, and management statements point the other way without disproving the claim. The evidence settles neither support nor contradiction.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition captures the three parts: AI hallucinates regularly, it is getting worse, and executives are adopting it as fast as possible regardless of fit. It drops the 'every appreciable part' phrasing, which changes little.

contract.note: Reading 'getting worse' as broad deterioration and the executive part as a broad pattern, not every executive, is ordinary and fair. The speaker gave no metric or baseline.

evidence.note: A May 2023 study finds ChatGPT and GPT-4 often give incorrect answers backed by false claims. This supports only the part about recurring hallucination.
Comparing March and June 2023 versions shows both regressions and improvements across tasks. It shows no broad deterioration and no stable performance either.
IBM's account of its own CEO survey shows strong uptake alongside concern about risks. It does not measure maximum-speed adoption or deployment despite known unsuitability.

reviews.rationale: Only the hallucination part is supported (e1). The study comparing model versions shows a mix of gains and losses, so broad deterioration is neither shown nor refuted. The survey does not establish adoption regardless of suitability. The compound claim as a whole cannot be settled.
